canonical_facts.adam_sexuality: Adam is openly gay from the novel's opening, not secretly hiding his identity from everyone. He is out at school and his family are aware or come to be aware. He states: 'I've known I was gay since I was thirteen. And what's more, I like it.' The bullying he faces is from hostile peers, not a secret he keeps from the world. After the attack he withdraws, but his sexuality was never a hidden secret in the way L3 and L6 describe.
canonical_facts.josh_role: Josh is one of Dante's friends. He is also Adam's boyfriend — but a deeply closeted, ashamed one who insists on keeping their relationship secret. Josh is not a symbol of acceptance; he is ashamed of Adam and of himself. Crucially, Josh is one of the three boys (Josh, Logan, Paul) who carry out the homophobic attack on Adam. Josh beats Adam severely while Logan and Paul hold Dante. He later apologises to Adam and turns himself in to the police.
canonical_facts.mothers_fate: The boys' mother did not 'leave' the family. She died of cancer. Tyler raised his sons alone after losing her to cancer. This is confirmed across multiple sources.
canonical_facts.emma_arrival: Emma does not arrive as a newborn. She arrives in a pushchair/buggy — sources describe her as approximately 10 months old. Melanie's deception is not 'placing Emma in Dante's arms' on the doorstep; Melanie asks Dante to mind Emma while she goes shopping and never returns, later texting to say she won't be coming back.
canonical_facts.dante_university_subject: Dante plans to study journalism at university.
canonical_facts.attack_detail: Adam is hospitalised in critical condition after the attack. Dante reports to the police what happened. The attackers are Josh, Logan, and Paul — all of Dante's friends. The attack occurs after a birthday celebration (Dante's 18th) at a pub called the Bar Belle. Paul later reveals that Logan engineered the attack to make Josh prove he was not gay.
canonical_facts.josh_ending: Josh is later revealed to be gay himself. He kisses Dante and reveals this. He apologises unreservedly to Adam and hands himself into the police.
canonical_facts.blackman_laureate: Blackman was Children's Laureate 2013–2015. Boys Don't Cry was published in 2010 — three years before her Laureate appointment.

findings.lesson_text: Adam is Dante's younger brother, still at school, and he is gay. He has known this about himself for some time, but he has told nobody in his family.
findings.issue: The lesson frames Adam as secretly hiding his sexuality from his family throughout the novel, which contradicts the canonical characterisation. Adam is openly gay from the novel's opening — he is out, bullied at school because of it, and his family is aware of or comes to discover his sexuality. He is not 'hiding' in the way described. His quote 'I've known I was gay since I was thirteen. And what's more, I like it' is uttered openly, not as a secret. The lesson's framing — 'he has told nobody in his family' — is a misreading that would lead students to make factually wrong claims in the exam.
findings.canonical_truth: Adam is openly gay from the start of the novel, faces bullying at school specifically because he is out. His sexuality is not a hidden secret from his family in the way the lesson describes. Multiple GCSE revision sources confirm Adam is 'openly gay' at the novel's opening.

findings.lesson_text: Josh is Adam's boyfriend, and their relationship offers Adam moments of genuine happiness and acceptance. However, it also increases the risk of exposure. Every time they are together in public, Adam is aware that being seen could trigger the bullying he already endures — or worse.
findings.issue: The lesson presents Josh as a supportive boyfriend who provides Adam with 'genuine happiness and acceptance'. This is critically misleading. Josh is deeply ashamed of Adam and of his own sexuality, demands secrecy, and eventually becomes one of the three boys who carry out the violent homophobic attack on Adam. Josh beats Adam severely while his friends hold Dante. Josh is simultaneously Adam's secret ex-boyfriend AND his attacker. Presenting Josh as a symbol of love and acceptance — without any mention that he is one of the perpetrators of the attack — creates a false and dangerous misrepresentation. Students who learn from this lesson would misattribute the novel's climax.
findings.canonical_truth: Josh is Dante's friend and Adam's secret boyfriend, but he is closeted and ashamed. He insists the relationship remain hidden. He is one of the three attackers (Josh, Logan, Paul) who assault Adam and Dante. Josh beats Adam severely. He later reveals he is gay himself, apologises to Adam, and turns himself in to the police.

findings.lesson_text: Key Fact: Josh's character serves a crucial function: he proves that Adam's sexuality is natural and healthy. Without Josh, Adam's storyline would only be about suffering. With Josh, Blackman shows that the problem is not Adam's identity — it is society's response to it.
findings.issue: This Key Fact box repeats the false framing that Josh is a positive presence in Adam's life, a vehicle for showing that Adam's sexuality is healthy. In reality, Josh is ashamed of his own sexuality, is one of the attackers, and is himself a product of internalised homophobia. Josh does not 'prove' Adam's sexuality is healthy — Josh's arc is about the destructive effects of shame and repression, not about validation of Adam's identity. The Key Fact is thematically wrong and factually misleading.
findings.canonical_truth: Josh's function in the novel is to demonstrate the damage caused by internalised homophobia and shame, not to validate Adam's identity. His relationship with Adam is secretive and ultimately leads to violence.

findings.lesson_text: When the doorbell rings, Dante expects the postman with his results. Instead, his ex-girlfriend Melanie is standing on the doorstep — holding a baby. She tells Dante that the child, Emma, is his daughter. The shock is total. Dante had no idea Melanie was pregnant, and she has kept the baby a secret for months. Melanie does not ask Dante if he wants to be involved; she simply places Emma in his arms and, within a short time, disappears from their lives.
findings.issue: The lesson presents Melanie as arriving, declaring Emma is Dante's daughter, placing the baby in his arms, and quickly disappearing. The novel's actual scene is different in two important respects: (1) Emma arrives in a pushchair/buggy, not as a held infant — she is approximately 10 months old, not a newborn; (2) Melanie's method of abandonment involves asking Dante to mind Emma while she 'goes shopping', and she never returns — later texting to say she won't be coming back. She does not announce on the doorstep that the baby is his. The lesson also later refers to 'caring for a newborn', which is factually incorrect.
findings.canonical_truth: Emma arrives in a pushchair/buggy — she is approximately 10 months old. Melanie's abandonment is deceptive: she asks Dante to babysit while she goes shopping, then disappears, later contacting him to say she will not return.

findings.lesson_text: Dante has just received his A-level results and plans to study at university
findings.issue: The lesson never specifies what Dante intends to study at university. The novel establishes that Dante plans to study journalism. This is a minor omission but could cost students a specific textual detail in their exam response.
findings.canonical_truth: Dante plans to study journalism at university. This is his specific ambition, not a generic university aspiration.

findings.lesson_text: He does not hesitate. His instinct is to protect his brother, regardless of the danger to himself. Blackman uses this moment to show that Dante's experience of caring for Emma has expanded his capacity for love and protectiveness beyond his own child. Crucially, Dante's protectiveness is not driven by traditional masculine aggression. He does not seek revenge or violence. Instead, he comforts Adam, takes him home and makes it clear that he accepts him completely.
findings.issue: The lesson says Dante 'comforts Adam, takes him home' after the attack. In the novel, Adam is hospitalised in critical condition — he is not taken home by Dante. Adam's injuries are severe enough to require hospitalisation. Additionally, Dante reports what happened to the police, which the lesson omits entirely. Students who learn from this account would misrepresent a key plot sequence in the exam.
findings.canonical_truth: Adam is rushed to hospital in critical condition after the attack. Dante reports to the police what happened. Adam does not go home; he is hospitalised. After the hospital, Adam withdraws, stays in his room, and becomes depressed/suicidal before ultimately recovering.

findings.lesson_text: Adam is attacked by a group of boys in a hate crime because of his sexuality.
findings.issue: The lesson refers only to 'a group of boys' without identifying the attackers. The fact that the attackers are Josh (Adam's former secret boyfriend), Logan and Paul — all Dante's friends — is central to the novel's thematic argument about internalised homophobia and complicity. That Josh, who was intimate with Adam, is one of his attackers is the novel's most devastating irony. Omitting this entirely means students miss the key thematic content of the climax.
findings.canonical_truth: The attackers are Josh, Logan, and Paul — all Dante's friends. Josh is Adam's former secret boyfriend. The attack is orchestrated by Logan, who pressures Josh to prove he is not gay. Josh beats Adam severely while Logan and Paul restrain Dante.

findings.lesson_text: Where Dante's crisis is visible and public (a baby cannot be hidden), Adam's crisis is internal and secret. He is gay, and he spends most of the novel terrified of being discovered.
findings.issue: This repeats the same mischaracterisation as L3. Adam is not 'terrified of being discovered' — he is openly gay and already targeted at school for it. His crisis is not about concealment; it is about navigating a hostile social environment while being openly who he is. The lesson's framing of Adam as secretly hiding his identity is inconsistent with the novel's text.
findings.canonical_truth: Adam is openly gay. He is bullied and attacked because he is openly gay, not because his secret is discovered. His challenge is surviving in a homophobic environment, not concealing his identity.

findings.lesson_text: Dad (Tyler Bridgeman Senior) Dad is one of Blackman's most complex and nuanced characters. He is a single father who has raised two boys alone after their mother left.
findings.issue: The lesson states the boys' mother 'left' the family. This is factually wrong. Their mother died of cancer. Tyler raised his sons alone after losing her to cancer. 'She left' implies voluntary abandonment and changes the entire meaning of Tyler's character arc — he is not a man abandoned by a partner, but a widower who has buried grief under stoicism and emotional control. Students who take this lesson's version into the exam will state incorrect facts about a core character's backstory.
findings.canonical_truth: The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler Bridgeman has raised Dante and Adam as a single parent after their mother's death. This is confirmed across multiple sources including the Berg's Book Club and Vulpes Libris reviews.

findings.lesson_text: Supporting Characters: Josh, Aunt Jackie and Collette. Josh is Adam's boyfriend and the novel's primary symbol of acceptance and normality. His presence proves that Adam's sexuality is natural and healthy — the problem lies with society, not with Adam. Josh also represents risk: their public relationship makes Adam a target.
findings.issue: This is the most seriously wrong passage in the unit. Josh is described as 'the novel's primary symbol of acceptance and normality'. Josh is the opposite: he is a closeted, ashamed character who is deeply conflicted about his own sexuality, insists his relationship with Adam remain hidden, and is one of the three boys who carry out the brutal attack on Adam. Characterising Josh as a symbol of acceptance directly inverts his function in the novel. A student using this description in an exam would demonstrate a fundamental misunderstanding of the text.
findings.canonical_truth: Josh is not a symbol of acceptance. He is closeted, ashamed of being gay, pressures Adam to keep their relationship secret, and is one of the three attackers (with Logan and Paul) who hospitalise Adam. He later reveals he is gay, apologises to Adam, and turns himself in to police. His arc is about internalised homophobia and its destructive consequences.

findings.lesson_text: Key Fact: The absent mother is never fully explained. Her departure shaped Dad's emotional guardedness and forced him into the role of sole carer.
findings.issue: The Key Fact uses the word 'departure' to describe the mother's absence, which implies she chose to leave. The mother died of cancer. Her death — not a departure or abandonment — is what shaped Tyler's grief-driven stoicism and emotional guardedness. The distinction matters: Tyler's entire characterisation as a man who cannot express vulnerability is rooted in unprocessed grief, not in being left by a partner.
findings.canonical_truth: The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler's emotional guardedness stems from suppressed grief over her death, not from being abandoned.

findings.lesson_text: The practicalities of caring for a newborn make it impossible.
findings.issue: Emma is referred to as a 'newborn' but she is not. She arrives in a pushchair and is approximately 10 months old. Calling her a newborn is a repeated factual inaccuracy across multiple lessons in this unit (also L2).
findings.canonical_truth: Emma arrives in a pushchair/buggy and is approximately 10 months old, not a newborn.
